blocks.text: Structural engineering training connects classroom principles with the practical interpretation of project drawings, loading assumptions, analysis models and design output. In a pre-engineered steel building, the geometry of the primary frames, the restraint provided by secondary steel and the behaviour of the connections must be considered together. This report presents a four-week study of these aspects using the project records supplied for a proposed PEB industrial building in Chennai.

The building has a plan dimension of 36 m × 72.2 m, a roof slope of 1:12, an analytical eave height of 10 m and a ridge height of 11.5 m. Ridge columns divide the roof into two 18 m horizontal spans. The structural system comprises tapered built-up steel columns and rafters, longitudinal hollow-section members, tension-only rod bracing, cold-formed secondary members and profiled roof and wall cladding. The supplied STAAD.Pro model contains 180 joints, 314 members and 38 pinned supports.

The first week covers preliminary project information, types of structures, design-load calculations and load cases. The second week explains the structural model, the analysis of members, shear force and bending moment diagrams, member forces and displacement checks. The third week addresses proportioning, member dimensions, strength and stability checks for columns, rafters, secondary steel and bracing, together with connection-design requirements. The fourth week covers general detailing notes, dimensioned arrangement drawings, member profiles and connection concepts.

The study is based on the supplied 68-page training PDF and R1_PEB.ANL analysis output. Calculations and recorded results are distinguished from illustrative teaching examples. Review of the analysis identified a load-combination discrepancy, two failed member checks and unresolved analysis/design warnings; these are documented in the technical chapters. No revised STAAD run or final connection/foundation design is claimed. The report provides a structured academic account of the design process, with demonstration personal details and drawings intended for training use.

blocks.text: 1.1 General

Structural engineering deals with the analysis and design of systems that transfer loads safely to the ground while providing suitable stiffness, stability and durability. For steel buildings, member resistance must be considered together with local buckling, overall stability, connection behaviour and the restraint available during construction and service. The design process therefore extends from understanding the project requirements to coordinating the analytical model with the drawings.

A pre-engineered building uses an engineered combination of primary frames, secondary members and cladding. Tapered built-up sections allow the distribution of steel to follow the structural demand. Repeated framing arrangements support efficient fabrication and erection, but the benefits depend on correctly defined loads, reliable connections and adequate bracing. This training report follows that process through the supplied PEB case study.
1.2 About the Project

The case study is a proposed industrial PEB with a 36 m transverse width and 72.2 m longitudinal length, giving a plan area of 2,599.2 m². Ten transverse frame lines form nine longitudinal bays. The two end bays are 8.1 m long and the seven intermediate bays are 8.0 m long. The analytical eaves are at 10.0 m and the ridge is at 11.5 m, consistent with a roof rise of 1.5 m and a slope of 1:12.

The model includes interior ridge columns and gable-end posts. Accordingly, the 36 m building width is not an unobstructed clear span: the roof is supported over two 18 m horizontal spans. The source input sheet states 9.5 m clear height, 0.47 mm Galvalume roof and wall sheeting, a 3 m brick-wall height and three canopy zones. The project particulars and member families are summarized in Chapter 2.
1.3 Location and Site Details

The supplied project input sheet identifies Chennai as the location. The wind and earthquake inputs adopted in the training records are reproduced in Chapter 3. A precise site address, site survey and geotechnical report were not supplied; soil bearing capacity, foundation dimensions and other site-specific information are therefore not assumed.
1.4 Type of Structure

The primary system consists of steel columns and rafters forming moment-resisting transverse frames. Longitudinal hollow-section members and roof/wall bracing provide the longitudinal load path. Purlins, girts and eave struts transfer cladding loads to the primary steel and provide restraint where designed. Column bases are modelled as pinned; they still transfer vertical force, horizontal shear and possible uplift.
[S1] project inputs and geometry, pp.1–4; [S2] joint coordinates, member incidences and support definitions. References are listed on page 24.
1.5 Objectives and Scope of the Training

The objectives are to understand the structural arrangement of a PEB; trace gravity and lateral load paths; calculate the design loads adopted in the source records; interpret analysis forces and displacements; explain proportioning and design checks for the main structural members; and prepare coherent design notes and study drawings. The scope covers the four weekly topics requested for the training report.

The study addresses columns, rafters, canopy beams, longitudinal struts, purlins, girts, rods and their connection requirements. Member checks available in the ANL are reported with their limitations. Components for which complete design information is unavailable are discussed through design procedures or clearly identified examples, rather than assigned unsupported sizes or pass results.
1.6 Methodology

The work follows six stages: (i) review the supplied training PDF and analysis output; (ii) extract project geometry, materials, member sizes and loading assumptions; (iii) reproduce representative load calculations; (iv) examine the model, forces, displacement summaries, code checks and warnings; (v) explain the design of primary and secondary members using source results and worked examples; and (vi) prepare a member schedule, arrangement drawings and connection concepts.

The numerical checks in this report are documentary and arithmetic checks of the supplied records. They are not a new structural analysis. In particular, an input correction requires a revised analysis before its effects on forces, member utilization or foundation reactions can be established.
1.7 Organization of the Report

Chapter 2 describes the project information and structural systems. Chapter 3 presents the first-week load calculations and combination register. Chapter 4 covers the second-week structural analysis and results. Chapter 5 explains third-week member proportioning and design. Chapter 6 presents fourth-week detailing notes and drawings. Chapter 7 concludes the study and provides the source register. The table of contents gives the page locations of individual sections.
1.8 Documentation and Evidence Basis

[S1] denotes the supplied file 1000016606.pdf, with references to its physical PDF pages. [S2] denotes R1_PEB.ANL, with references to numbered input commands or printed STAAD pages. [R1–R4] denote the external technical references listed in Chapter 7. “Calculated” identifies arithmetic from stated inputs; “illustrative” identifies a teaching example; and “recorded” identifies a result transcribed from the supplied analysis.

The cover uses demonstration student, institution, company and supervisor details, as requested. These entries do not certify attendance or site visits. The report retains the source’s design findings, including the failed checks and unresolved warnings, and the drawing sheets are marked for training use.
2.1 Preliminary Information and Structural Systems

A PEB combines engineered primary frames with repetitive secondary members and profiled cladding. Built-up tapered sections allow the depth to vary with the force pattern. Shop-fabricated components are assembled on site, commonly using bolted field connections. The selected structural arrangement must also accommodate openings, drainage, services and erection stability.

4.1 Structural Model and Analysis Procedure

The model is a three-dimensional STAAD SPACE frame with 180 joints, 314 beam members and 38 pinned supports. Global X is across the 36 m width, Y is vertical and Z is along the 72.2 m length. Pins restrain translations and release support rotations; the bases still transfer vertical force, horizontal shear and possible uplift.

blocks.text: 4.1.1 Analysis sequence and interpretation

The study sequence is: establish geometry and connectivity; assign material and section properties; define supports, releases and restraints; apply loads; solve; check equilibrium and deformation; extract member forces; and complete strength and serviceability checks. Gravity flows from sheeting to purlins, rafters, columns and foundations. Longitudinal wind flows through the roof/wall bracing system to restrained bases.

The supplied run uses PERFORM ANALYSIS and shows tension/compression iterations for primary cases. It then uses LOAD COMB to combine results. Bentley explains that tension-only behaviour and second-order effects require simultaneous combined loading, normally using appropriate REPEAT LOAD cases, rather than superposition of separate results [R3]. Re-analysis is therefore a necessary follow-up.
[S2] printed pp.1–8 and commands 129–163, 303; [R3].

title: 4.2 SHEAR FORCE AND BENDING MOMENT DIAGRAMS

blocks.text: Shear force describes the transverse force transmitted across a cut; bending moment describes the internal couple. For a downward UDL w and the usual sagging-positive beam convention, dV/dx = −w and dM/dx = V. Thus a constant UDL gives a straight shear diagram and a parabolic moment diagram. Diagram signs must be distinguished from STAAD local member-end sign conventions.

blocks.text: 4.3.1 Engineering interpretation

The eave region carries substantial frame moment and shear, which explains the increased column/rafter depths near the joint. Ridge-side rafter 39 is close to its recorded shear resistance. The ridge columns reverse between compression and tension across the load set and also develop large moments. The canopy behaves as a cantilever connected to the main column system.

The reported PASS of the longitudinal SHS member is accompanied by a second-order-analysis warning. The failed ridge-column checks are governed by LC118, whose input factor is inconsistent with its title. A revised analysis may change both forces and utilization; no revised pass/fail outcome is inferred here.
4.4.1 Primary-case displacement summary

The ANL reports translations in centimetres; they are converted below to millimetres. Each cell gives the signed reported extreme followed by its node number. Different component extremes generally occur at different nodes, so these entries cannot be combined as one displacement vector or directly added to form a service combination.
4.4.2 Serviceability interpretation

The PDF separately illustrates 52.3 mm lateral movement against 10,000/150 = 66.7 mm, and 9.844 mm vertical rafter movement against 18,000/180 = 100 mm [S1, p.57]. Those values are not established as service envelopes of this ANL run. They are retained only as training-slide examples. Actual limits depend on cladding, supported finishes, use, connection details and the adopted design specification.

For final checking, obtain nodal and member displacements for each service combination, including the relative vertical deflection of rafters between their moving supports. Check purlins/girts, canopy tips, frame sway, gutter falls and drainage separately. A primary-case joint displacement is not a complete member-deflection check.
4.4.3 Equilibrium and warnings

These aggregate balances support force equilibrium for the printed cases. They do not validate the assumed loads, member restraints or nonlinear combinations. Individual foundation reaction envelopes are still required, including coincident shear and uplift.

5.1 Proportioning and Member-Size Schedule

Proportioning starts from the force path, frame geometry and restraint conditions. Deeper sections are placed where bending demand is high; flange area resists bending/axial action, while the web transfers shear and stabilizes the flanges. Economy depends on plate thickness, fabrication repetition, transport limits, local buckling and serviceability, not only on section area.
5.1.1 Reading the tapered-section input

The seven TAPERED values are Dstart, tw, Dend, btop, ttop, bbottom and tbottom [R4]. D is the overall section depth; clear web depth is D − ttop − tbottom. Equal flanges are assigned in the listed families. Start/end follow the member incidence order, so the schedule must not be reversed during fabrication interpretation.

For a symmetric I section: A = 2btf + (D − 2tf)tw.
For D = 524, b = 275, tf = 12, tw = 5 mm: A = 9,100 mm² = 91.0 cm².

This is a schedule of analytical section assignments, not an approved fabrication bill. Original PDF elevation notes and the ANL are not assumed to be the same revision. Main-roof purlins are represented through applied loads; their sizes and checks need the separate secondary-member design described on p.18.

A low axial-force ratio alone does not establish adequacy under frame bending.

title: 5.3 DESIGN OF RAFTERS AND CANOPY BEAMS

blocks.text: 5.3.1 Rafter design principles

A rafter check begins with plate classification and the compression-flange restraint under each load direction. Gravity and wind uplift can reverse the compression flange. Purlins connected to the upper flange do not automatically restrain the lower flange; flange stays and their connection/load path must be designed. Slender webs require explicit treatment of shear buckling and flexural resistance.

For a suitable laterally supported section: Md = βb Zp fy / γm0, subject to code limits.
For a semi-compact section βb Zp corresponds to Ze.
For an unrestrained member: Md depends on lateral-torsional buckling strength.
Shear yielding reference: Vd = Av fy / (√3 γm0); reduce/check for shear buckling where applicable.

These are design frameworks, not a replacement for the slender-web and high-shear rules applicable to the supplied sections. Bending resistance can reduce when shear is high, and axial–moment interaction must be checked using concurrent forces.

blocks.text: 5.5.2 Connection design method

Extract the concurrent N, V and M at each joint for every governing case, including reversal. Select a connection arrangement that provides the stiffness/release assumed in the model. Check bolts in shear, tension and interaction; bearing, net section and block shear of connected plates; end-plate bending and prying; weld strength; and column/rafter local effects. An initial moment-couple estimate is T ≈ M/z, but actual bolt-row distribution and prying must be analysed.

For a pinned base, determine compression bearing, uplift anchorage and shear transfer consistently with the assumed rotational release. Foundation design then checks soil pressure, sliding, overturning, uplift, concrete bending, shear and punching. Site soil data, concrete grade, embedment, anchor grade and base reactions are not supplied; foundation dimensions are therefore not invented.
5.5.3 Steel quantity reported by the model

Total reported model steel weight = 775.328 kN.
Equivalent mass using g = 9.81 m/s² ≈ 79.03 tonnes.
Model mass / plan area ≈ 79,034 / 2,599.2 = 30.41 kg/m².

This is the weight of the members represented in the model. Main-roof purlins and much of the girt/eave-strut system are accounted for as applied loading rather than explicit steel members. Connections, base plates, stiffeners, coating, sheeting and procurement waste are not established by this take-off. The 15% self-weight load factor is not a measured connection quantity.

Week 3 deliverable: a traceable member schedule and explanation of design checks across all structural families. The source is insufficient for a complete approved building design; missing checks are identified rather than replaced with invented pass results.

blocks.text: 6.1 General Notes for Design and Detailing

The following notes form a training specification to accompany the study drawings. They translate analysis assumptions into drawing requirements. Final material grades, tolerances, connection sizes and inspection criteria must be assigned by the responsible designer and project specification.

rows: All drawing dimensions are in millimetres unless stated. Levels relate to the model base datum. Do not scale drawings. Verify site dimensions and openings before fabrication.
Primary member design values are fy = 345 MPa and fu = 490 MPa; SHS and rod values differ. Specify the actual product grade, thickness-dependent strength and certificates in procurement documents.
Show flange/web thicknesses, taper direction, plate joints, weld symbols and stiffeners. Analytical division points do not automatically represent physical splices.
Specify bolt grade, diameter, hole type, spacing, edge distances and tightening method. Show end plates, cleats, gussets, base plates and anchor projections with design references.

Show weld type, size, effective length and required continuity. Use approved welding procedures; inspect as required by the project quality plan. Do not prescribe unverified weld sizes from this report.

Locate purlin/girt attachments, flange stays, sag rods and braces explicitly. Verify the compression-flange restraint under gravity and uplift. A 1.5 m software length requires a corresponding physical restraint system.
Identify permanent braced bays and connections. Provide a planned erection sequence and temporary stability system; do not assume partially assembled frames are stable.
Coordinate anchors, pedestal levels, grout, base rotation assumptions and foundation reactions. Model pins do not remove uplift or horizontal shear demand.
Coordinate sheet laps, screws, flashings, gutters and downpipes. Check local suction zones, openings and water accumulation; prevent incompatible restraint at expansion interfaces.
Define preparation, coating/galvanizing and touch-up requirements for the exposure. Avoid water traps and inaccessible unprotected joints; coordinate fire protection where required.

7.1 Learning Outcomes, Conclusions and References
7.1.1 Weekly learning outcomes

Week 1: interpreted the project geometry, distinguished frame types and reproduced gravity, wind and earthquake load calculations. Week 2: explained the model, plotted reference shear/moment diagrams and interpreted member forces, displacement summaries and equilibrium. Week 3: documented section proportions and studied compression, bending, shear, bracing and secondary-member design. Week 4: prepared general notes, arrangement drawings, member profiles and connection design concepts.
7.1.2 Conclusion and remaining engineering work

The records support a useful study of a tapered steel PEB with ridge-supported roof frames. They also show why analysis output must be reviewed before drawing a design conclusion. The most significant findings are the LC118 factor discrepancy, inappropriate result superposition for tension-only behaviour, two failed ridge-column checks, second-order warnings, web-thickness warnings and incomplete design coverage for rods, secondary steel and connections.

The next engineering revision should confirm the adopted code editions and project loads; reconcile wind zones, seismic mass and load directions; correct and rerun the model using appropriate combined loading and second-order treatment; then complete strength/serviceability checks, connections, anchors and foundations. The report does not claim that these corrections have already been made.
